body.p: REMARKS
This communication is responsive to the Office Action dated October 30, 2023.
Applicant has canceled claims 16 and 17. Claims 1 - 5, 8 - 15, and 18 - 22 remain pending upon entry of this communication.

In the Office Action, the Examiner noted that 35 U.S.C. § 112 (f) has not been invoked when interpreting claims 21 because "means for sensing," "means for determining," and means for selecting" "refers to one or more processors." Applicant acknowledges the Examiner's interpretation under 35 U.S.C. § 112 (f).
Claim Rejection Under 35 U.S.C. 4 112

In the Office Action, the Examiner rejected claims 1-5 and 8-22 under 35 U.S.C. § 112, first paragraph, asserting that claims 1-5 and 8-22 are not supported by Applicant's specification. The Examiner asserted that "the independent claims, the specification fails to provide adequate written description for a method or a system comprising one or more processors configured to select a first frequency band of interest and a second frequency band of interest, and one or more processors configured to control therapy delivery by a medical device based on determined first and second biomarkers."2
As discussed in the Amendment in Response to Office Action filed August 14, 2023,

Applicant disagrees. As noted previously, Applicant's specification explicitly states that that the processing circuitry may determine, "one or more frequency bands of interest using any suitable technique."3 One of ordinary skill in the art would not have interpreted determining one or more frequency bands of interest as ONLY "select a first frequency band of interest," as characterized by the Examiner.
Similarly, Applicant's specification explicitly states that the "pattern of the power
distribution over one or more frequency sub-bands indicative of a particular patient state can be within the same frequency band or over one or more frequency bands."4 Applicant's

specification further states, "sensing module 66 includes a frequency selective sensing circuit that extracts the energy level within one or more selected frequency bands and sub-bands of a sensed patient parameter signal, which may be, for example, a bioelectrical brain signal."5 Applicant's specification also describes, "the one or more frequency band characteristics meet a particular set of criteria (e.g., a particular spectral pattern) associated with the biomarker."6 From at least these portions Applicant's specification, along with Applicant's FIG. 9 as discussed in the previous response, Applicant's originally filed patent application clearly describes "the claimed invention in sufficient detail that one skilled in the art can reasonably conclude that the inventor had possession of the claimed invention."7

Specifically, from at least the excerpts from Applicant's written description above, one or ordinary skill in the art would have understood that Applicant's specification reciting "one or more frequency bands of interest" is evidence that the inventors had, at the time of filing, possession of "selecting a first frequency band of interest" and "selecting a second frequency band of interest," as recited by claim 1. Moreover, though not explicitly claimed, one of ordinary skill in the art would have understood that selecting one or more frequency bands of interest further includes selecting a third frequency band of interest, selecting a fourth frequency band of interest, selecting a fifth frequency band interest and so on.

Accordingly, for at least the reasons discussed above, Applicant independent claims are supported by Applicant's specification, in accordance with 35 U.S.C. § 112(a). Applicant respectfully requests reconsideration and withdrawal of all rejections under 35 U.S.C. § 112(a).

For at least these reasons, Applicant's current patent application is an application which is also disclosed in the prior application (the parent or original nonprovisional application or provisional application). The disclosure of the invention in the parent application and in the current application comply with the requirements of 35 U.S.C. § 112. Accordingly, Applicant's originally claim for priority is correct.

The Office Action rejected claims 16 and 17 under 35 U.S.C. § 112, second paragraph, as being indefinite for failing to particularly point out and distinctly claim the subject matter which the inventor or joint inventor regards as the invention. Specifically, the Office Action stated claims 16 and 17 do not further limit claim 11 from which claims 16 and 17 depend. Applicant

In the Office Action, the Examiner rejected claims 1-5 and 8-22 under 35 U.S.C. § 103(a) as allegedly being unpatentable over U.S. Patent Application Publication No. 2009/0082691 by Denison et al. (hereinafter, "Denison") in view of U.S. Patent Application Publication No. 2007/0197930 by Sarkela (hereinafter, "Sarkela") as evidenced by U.S. Patent No. 5,601,090 by Musha (hereinafter, "Musha"), further in view of U.S. Patent Application Publication No. 2008/0228100 by Navakatikyan (hereinafter, "Navakatikyan"). Applicant respectfully traverses the rejections. The applied references, alone or in any combination, do not disclose or suggest the subject matter defined by Applicant's claims, and there would have been no apparent reason that would have caused one of ordinary skill in the art to modify the applied references to arrive at the claimed subject matter.
The Examiner cited to Navakatikyan to correct an admitted deficiency of Denison in

view of Sarkela to disclose or suggest "one or more of a peak width less than or equal to a first threshold value or a peak width greater than or equal to a second threshold value" as recited by Applicant's claim 1, for example. The Examiner characterized Navakatikyan as "identifying a biomarker comprising a unimodal peak or a bimodal peak."8 Contrary to the Examiner's characterization, Navakatikyan instead describes calculations to determine, "the amplitude of a peak and a trough in each data group,"9 which includes determining "the time interval between the peak and/or the trough."10 Navakatikyan does not describe identifying a biomarker. Further, Navakatikyan does not describe, and Applicant's claim 1 does not recite, "identifying whether a variability in the amplitude (unimodal peak) of one or more frequency sub-bands exhibits a relatively high or low level of activity."11

The Examiner further asserted that a unimodal or a bimodal peak "inherently has a peak width greater than a threshold value (the threshold value being zero)."12 The Examiner's interpretation of the threshold being zero is not reasonable because then there is no peak. In other

words, the one or more processors would be unable to even determine a peak width if there is no peak. The Examiner's interpretation of a threshold being zero so that there is no peak to even have a peak width, removes this claim term from the claim and is thus not a reasonable interpretation.
Moreover, even assuming for the sake of argument that an interpretation that a zero

threshold is not unreasonable, Denison, in view of Sarkela and further in view of Navakatikyan does not disclose or suggest the subject matter of Applicant's claim 1, for example, "a peak width less than or equal to a first threshold value or a peak width greater than or equal to a second threshold value," because Navakatikyan never compares a peak width to a threshold. Instead Navakatikyan describes "the base level for determining amplitude is a line connecting the troughs either side of said peak and the base level for determining trough amplitude is a line connecting the peaks either side of said trough."13 Navakatikyan futher describes that "numerical values indicative of amplitude and interval difference are combined in predetermined ratios to provide said predetermined criteria."14 However, Navakatikyan never determines "one or more of a peak width less than or equal to a first threshold value or a peak width greater than or equal to a second threshold value," as recited by claim 1. For at least these reasons, the cited references alone or in any reasonable combination, do not disclose or suggest the subject matter defined by Applicant's claim 1, and there would have been no apparent reason that would have caused one of ordinary skill in the art to modify the applied references to arrive at the claimed subject matter. Independent claims 11, 21, and 22 include subject similar to that recited by claim
1 and arguments with regard to claim 1 apply equally to independent claims 11, 21, and 22.
For at least the reasons discussed above, independent claims 1, 11, 21, and 22 are
patentable over the cited references. The dependent claims incorporate the requirements of the respective independent claims.15 Accordingly, the dependent claims are likewise patentable.

For at least these reasons, the Examiner has failed to establish a primafacie case for non- patentability of Applicant's claims under 35 U.S.C. § 103. Applicant therefore respectfully requests reconsideration and withdrawal of all rejections under 35 U.S.C. § 103.

CONCLUSION
All claims in this application are in condition for allowance. Applicant does not

acquiesce as to any assertion in the Office Action with respect to the cited art or to Applicant's claims. Applicant's silence with respect to any assertion in the Office Action should not be interpreted as Applicant's acquiescence thereto. Applicant reserves the right to comment further with respect to the applied references and any pending claim in a future Amendment, Response, or on appeal. Applicant respectfully requests reconsideration and prompt allowance of all pending claims.

Applicant does not concede that the subject matter encompassed by the claims prior to this Response is unpatentable over the art cited by the Office Action. While several distinctions have been noted over the art of record, Applicant notes that there may be several other limitations that are neither taught nor suggested by the art of record. Applicant expressly reserves all rights and arguments with respect to distinctions not explicitly noted herein. In addition, to the extent that amendments included herein constitute a narrowing of the claims, such narrowing of the claims should not be construed as an admission as to the merits of the prior rejections. Indeed, Applicant traverses the rejections and preserves all rights and arguments. To the extent that any particular statement or argument by the Office in the pending Office Action has not been explicitly addressed herein, the same should not be construed as an acquiescence or admission by the Applicant that such statements or arguments by the Office are accurate and proper.
